members.tone: Skill first, deceit second - it can admire the craft even while it disapproves.
Homely and old, and the craft is entirely in the deceiving.
Skill in deceiving, and the skill is half admired - the disapproval is real but not total.
Suspicion rather than accusation - it says a thing is not to be trusted without saying what is wrong with it.
The animal metaphor - deceit with the fox's reputation for it.
Formal - the deceiving is deliberate and rather cold.
Names the person a knave - archaic, with a costume-drama ring.
The deception is in the smoothness - nothing catches, which is what makes it suspect.
The everyday word, and the one that emphasises secrecy over skill.
Playful rather than dangerous: mischief with a literary air.
A warning - the skill is in deceiving you.
Cunning with the disapproval taken out - a wily negotiator is being complimented.
*Don't get cute with me* - charm deployed as a manoeuvre.
Affectation as a whole manner - too studied to be trusted.
The intent is sustained and concealed, which is worse than a single trick.
The furthest word here: plotting as an ongoing occupation.
Mercy was available and was withheld; that is the entire charge.
Mercy named only as the thing withheld - slightly more formal than 'merciless'.
Ruthlessness named as a killer's - condemnation with half a boast inside it.
No quarter given - ruthlessness the word does not soften.
Pitiless - ruthlessness with no mercy left in it.
*A mortal enemy* - deadly rather than pitiless, and archaic in flavour.
Final and total - it fits weather and landscape as well as people, and is just as cold either way.
Adds the aftermath: there was no regret once it was done.
The everyday word - it makes the absence of pity a settled character, not a lapse.
The flat negative form - it names the missing pity without heat of its own.
Fierceness by animal comparison, which softens it into a figure of speech.
Settled rather than delighted; it describes a steady state, not a mood.
The plainest form, and it can shade toward settling - satisfied because one has stopped asking.
Contentment that should have been alarm - the danger was there to be seen.
The satisfaction is with oneself, and it is visible to everyone else.
The formal doubling of the same fault, and stiffer for it.
Closest to neutral here - a condition met rather than a character described.
The social version: pleasure in being right, worn where others can see it.
Descriptive and mild - it names an absence rather than an offence.
Rural coarseness, bookish enough to sound like a judgement from a distance.
Faults a lack of training or knowledge - mild, closer to pity than to scorn.
The farming metaphor is intact: nothing was planted here.
Sharper, because culture is treated as something the person declined to acquire.
Ill-manners as a settled character, and contemptible with it.
Young, male and physical - the lout takes up space and does not apologise.
Denies the person their own century; the insult is evolutionary.
The alternative spelling, equally cutting.
Clumsiness and stupidity together, with no suggestion it could be helped.
The animal comparison again, here about manners rather than appetite.
Rough-grained manners - it suggests a person left unfinished.
Pure class contempt - the word says more about the speaker than the subject.
Nearly forgiving: the material is good, the finishing was never done.
Harsher than 'rough-cut': the missing refinement read as offensive in itself.
Coarseness with class in it - the offence is against taste as much as manners.
The everyday word, and gentler than it looks - it blames inexperience, not intellect.
The French spelling, used when the writer wants a touch of distance.
Warm. It keeps the simplicity and drops the accusation.
Describes the face rather than the judgement; it can be wonder or it can be folly.
Slightly comic - the eyes wide with belief.
Faintly mocking - the credulity is what is being pointed at.
Dangerous - the compliment sits next to an insult, and the word does not say which it means.
Names the mechanism: this person believes things on insufficient evidence.
Defines the person by what can be done to them, which is why it stings.
Inexperience with an expiry date: a state to be grown out of, not a fault.
The plain accusation - it implies a history of being fooled.
Praise with a shadow: the same word can mean unspoiled or unprepared.
Frankness without calculation - the innocence is credited, not mocked.
The harshest here, and it borrows the vocabulary of disability to do its work.
Formal and faintly condescending - sophistication is assumed to be the goal.
Can be reproach or admiration, depending entirely on what the world is thought to be worth.
The plain word, and the one that has to be earned rather than displayed.
Wisdom claimed without limit, which is why it turns sarcastic so easily.
The technical form, at home in theology and in narration.
Sharpness of perception; it praises the seeing rather than the knowing.
Formal and warm - wisdom shown as insight rather than learning.
Latinate and cool - wisdom observed from a distance rather than warmly praised.
Appearance only. The owl looks wise; that is the whole of its claim.
Lofty, theological approval - wisdom of the godly kind rather than everyday shrewdness.
Wisdom that came with age, and the noun stands just behind the adjective.
A habit of overriding others, described from the outside.
Political, and it scales from a parent to a state without changing meaning.
Borrows a form of government to describe a manner; the comparison is the insult.
The weight metaphor is exact - the other person is pressed down, not persuaded.
Power exercised alone, and answerable to nobody.
The mildest in the family - it belittles the manner rather than condemning the power.
Faults the manner more than the strength - self-assurance exercised as power nobody granted.
Mock-grand, and the mockery is doing the condemning.
Authority assumed rather than earned - the offence is in the presumption.
It allows no reply, which is the whole of the offence.
Noise without much force behind it; more ridiculous than frightening.
Names harm rather than manner - the browbeating of others is the point.
Disregard worn lightly, as though the other person's stake were not real.
A decision taken over someone's head, with no thought of asking.
Force without proportion - more was applied than the thing needed.
*Ride roughshod over* - disregard rather than violence; the shoes are the image.
Restraint doing the work - the highest praise in the family, and the quietest.
Elegance turned into a project, and visibly so.
Vanity of dress as a character trait - the dandy made an adjective.
Beyond dandified: the appearance has crowded out everything else.
A marketing word more than a compliment - it still sounds like packaging.
The spaced spelling, slightly more formal than 'deluxe'.
Clipped and fashion-trade; it names a look rather than a quality.
In this sense, genuine praise - refinement noticed and credited.
Pretension built in - it announces a rank rather than showing one.
Sneers at the elegance as put on - the height is affectation.
Praise at the limit, and it implies the observer noticed every detail.
Rare and studied. Whether that is praise depends on how hard the search shows.
Luxury with a raised eyebrow: elegance that announces its own price.
Grooming and polish rather than taste; it is about the finish.
Admiring: polish so complete the effort disappears.
The plain word, and a small complaint - it expects the state to be temporary.
About too many things rather than dirt; a cluttered desk can still be working.
Disorder seen as rubbish - the mess condemned, whatever left it.
Disorder that suggests something happened - the state was not chosen.
The British spelling, identical in force.
Archaic and comic-sounding; using it is a decision.
The gentlest word in the family - rumpled clothes are forgiven, and sometimes liked.
Disorder that flatters - untidiness that can be arranged on purpose.
Disorder as a fault - the word has the ring of an offence.
The sound is the meaning, and it is far too cheerful to condemn much.
Archaic and comic - disorder with an air of the furtive about it.
Order was lost rather than never present - the pieces are all still there.
The plain claim that there is no gap between what is felt and what is said.
Legal Latin, and it is about standing rather than feeling.
Sincerity at intensity - a cordial loathing is as heartfelt as a cordial welcome.
Earnestness at full warmth - a wish held close to the heart.
Earnestness with full weight behind it - a devout wish is meant, not merely said.
Sincerity that shows its effort, which is why it can be faintly comic.
Earnest and unadorned - it stakes the speaker's own sincerity on the feeling.
The broadest word in the family and the one with the most to lose.
Tests the thing against a counterfeit - it presumes fakes are in circulation.
Unfeigned rather than merely accurate - the feeling is as real as it looks.
Defined against pretence, which is a curious way to have to say it.
Nothing held back and nothing divided; slightly archaic.
Devotion offered entire - nothing held back.
The most emphatic form - devotion offered with the whole self.
Endurance with an even temper - the temper is what distinguishes it from mere waiting.
Patience aimed at work, and it praises the steadiness rather than the result.
The same steadiness against resistance; it presumes there was reason to stop.
Praise for the bearing - the wrongs are continual and the patience holds.
Faintly complaining on the person's behalf - the trouble should have ended by now.
Restraint under provocation, when retaliation was available and was declined.
The Latinate form of *long-suffering*, and almost extinct.
Endurance credited as a virtue - hardship borne without complaint.
A construction rather than a word - *patient of delay* - and formal to the point of stiffness.
Describes the pace and lets the character be inferred.
